prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After reading the full first-round exchange, I still place B001 first, and I have tried to test it rather than inherit it from the unanimous opening. The discovery is specific: proglucagon processing, the truncated active GLP-1(7-36) amide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic, glucagonostatic and satiety actions, and the receptor pathway. It changed the field in a way that is discernible and no longer speculative, because decades of independent human physiology and large outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease have confirmed it. The chair's observation that round 2 should test attribution more than the headline is right, and it is where my own thinking has moved: not on whether B001 deserves the prize, but on how firmly the citation should be anchored in physiology. A prize to Holst for human incretin physiology, Drucker for GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and the receptor pathway, and Mojsov for identification and synthesis of the active peptide credits the discovery chain and fits a prize for physiology or medicine. I keep a single-achievement prize because the three-person cap would otherwise split the slots and weaken both parts.
statement.case_against: The reservation I weigh most is still attribution, and I want to be plain that it has not been resolved by the discussion. Every member, including me, relies on general knowledge for the division of priority between Mojsov and Habener's group, and nothing in the supplied files lets us settle it. Knudsen's acylation chemistry is what produced the long-acting drugs, so a physiology trio can be read as honouring the hormone rather than the therapy. I accept that criticism but think it is answered by the citation wording, which names the therapeutic consequence without crediting the drug design. The cap forces an exclusion in either direction, and whoever is left out has a real claim. If the committee found the priority question for the active peptide to be genuinely unresolvable on documents, my preferred trio would be weakened and I would want to revisit the configuration instead of defending it by default.

responses.point: El Manira named Holst, Drucker and Knudsen as the fallback if Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is judged too unclear, and called that a substantive change rather than a detail.
responses.response: I agree it would be a substantive change, and I think it is the right way to frame the choice. My difficulty is that the fallback swaps a contested discovery claim for a contested conceptual frame. It moves the prize from a physiology citation to one that has to carry both discovery and drug design, and then Mojsov's identification of the active form goes uncredited even if it is correct. Unless the committee can show from documents, not recollection, that her claim fails, I would keep her. If it could be shown to fail, I would take Holst, Drucker and Knudsen over a trio with a hole in the discovery chain, and I want that condition stated openly and not left implicit.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers a single-achievement prize because a second part would split the laureate slots and dilute both, and he names B017 or B012 as the safer outcome if B001 stalls on credit.
responses.response: I agree on the single part and I have no reason to add a second one. A split of three slots would leave a one- or two-person B001 that omits a discoverer who is already contested. I would, however, put B017 and B012 in a different light from his 'safer' description. Both have bigger credit problems than B001: Eshhar and other early receptor designers sit outside the B017 names, and B012 needs a principled cut from six to three. A runner-up is not an easier prize, and B001 stalling on one name would not make either of them the cleaner choice.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asks what rule would cut B012 from six names to three, and notes that he would hold B012 for a later year unless one is agreed. He also asks whether clinical translation should carry the same weight for mechanistic candidates such as B012.
responses.response: I do not see a rule that survives scrutiny. 'Discovery of the light-gated channel' points to Bamberg, Nagel and Hegemann. 'Deployment in neurons' points to Boyden and Deisseroth with Miesenboeck, and neither rule can be defended against the other. I therefore keep B012 as an alternative only. On translation, I would apply the same standard to every mechanism-led candidate and not wave B012 through as a tool because the field is large. My answer to the chair's question is that translation is evidence of maturity and not a requirement, which is why B001, with both, is stronger than B012 or B051 this year.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked the unfolded protein response (B051) second as conceptually original, and argued that the attribution doubts over B001 are a reason to deliberate over names and not to demote the discovery.
responses.response: On his second point we agree: the attribution doubts are a reason to deliberate, not to abandon B001, and I am deliberating rather than demoting. On B051 I hold my earlier view that Walter and Mori without the PERK/eIF2alpha branch make an incomplete citation, and that disease-level consequences are still being worked out. I do accept that three decades of textbook standing make it mature, which I said earlier, and that in a year with no stronger basic-science candidate it would be a legitimate prize. This year it competes with a case that has both mechanism and verified impact.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius warned that B001 is the obvious choice and that obviousness should not substitute for scrutiny of the credit, and she suggested that if the drug-development arm is the heart of the achievement, the preferred trio is wrong.
responses.response: I take that warning seriously and it is the point I have worked hardest on. I do not read the heart of the achievement as the drug design. Liraglutide and semaglutide were engineered to a mechanism that Holst, Drucker and Mojsov had defined, and the prize tradition I understand treats the discovery as the step that opened the field. The drug-development view is the strongest argument against my trio, and I do not find it decisive, since the citation can name the therapeutic consequence without crediting drug design. Where I would concede ground is a precise wording that says 'established the basis for', not 'led to', so that the citation does not overclaim.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can document, and not merely recall, how priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide divides between Mojsov and Habener's group. If it cannot, I do not know whether naming Mojsov is safe.
Whether a physiology-led citation will be accepted as honouring the therapy when Knudsen's acylation work is not credited.

If B001 stalls on attribution, whether B017 or B012 would be the more defensible fallback. I rank B017 first because its credit problem (Eshhar, Rosenberg's role) is easier to bound than a six-to-three cut.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B001 or for my alternatives B017 and B012. I disclose co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira on work unrelated to any shortlisted candidate, and past co-authorship with Ronald Evans from my Salk period on nuclear receptors, which does not involve any candidate here. I do not infer ties from shared institutions or from my own field of nuclear receptors and dopamine-neuron development.
